headline: A 2014 federal law that strengthens protections for children in foster care at risk of sex trafficking and makes changes to adoption incentives, child support enforcement, and foster care rules.
what_it_does: The law requires states that run foster care programs to identify, document, and report children and youth they believe are victims or at risk of sex trafficking, and to locate and respond when foster children run away. It lets foster children take part in age-appropriate activities under a "reasonable and prudent parent" standard, and it gives children age 14 and older a bigger role in planning their own cases. It also requires certain documents to be given to youth who leave foster care at 18, extends the adoption incentive program, and makes changes to international and tribal child support enforcement.

who_it_affects.group: Children and youth in foster care
who_it_affects.how: They gain a larger role in planning their own cases, a right to take part in age-appropriate activities, and a required set of documents when they leave care at 18 or an older age the state chooses.

They must be given a copy of their birth certificate, Social Security card, health insurance information, medical records, and a state ID or driver's license before discharge, unless they were in care less than six months.
They must create policies to identify and document child sex trafficking victims, report instances to law enforcement, and respond to children who run away.

who_it_affects.group: Foster parents and child care institutions
who_it_affects.how: They must apply the reasonable and prudent parent standard to children's activity decisions, and institutions must have a designated caregiver on site.

who_it_affects.group: Adoptive parents and states receiving adoption incentive payments
who_it_affects.how: The adoption incentive program is extended through fiscal year 2016, with changed payment formulas and a longer period to spend the funds.

who_it_affects.group: Parents and families in child support cases, including those in other countries and Indian tribes
who_it_affects.how: Tribes gain access to the Federal Parent Locator Service, and foreign child support agencies can get access and use federal tax refund collection for certain requests.
